title: Async: concurrency with deferreds
body: Jane Street's Async library runs many tasks on one thread by never blocking. An `'a Deferred.t` is a value that will be available later. `let%bind x = e in body` waits for `e` and then runs `body`, and `let%map x = e in v` transforms the eventual result. The scheduler runs other ready tasks while something waits, so one slow timer does not stop the rest.

Sequencing and concurrency are different choices. Chaining `let%bind a = f () in let%bind b = g () in ...` runs `g` only after `f` finishes. To run tasks at the same time, start them all first and then wait: `Deferred.all [ f (); g (); h () ]` returns the results in input order, whatever order they complete in.

Async is cooperative. A long computation without a `bind` blocks every other task, because nothing can preempt it. Use it for IO-bound work such as sockets and timers, and use domains (a later lesson) for CPU-bound parallelism. `Command.async` runs your deferred until it finishes and then exits.
challenge: src/timers.ml runs its three timers one after another. Change `run` so they start together with `Deferred.all` and print in completion order (fast, medium, slow) while the final summary still lists the results in input order.
projectInstructions: Build with `dune build --root .` and run `dune exec --root . bin/main.exe`. Compare the order of the printed names. Edit only src/timers.ml.
question: What does `Deferred.all [a; b; c]` return its results in?
correct: The order of the input list, regardless of which deferred completes first
reasoning: Deferred.all waits for every deferred and builds the result list positionally, so concurrency does not reorder it.
